The MOTC Highway Bureau creates an Uber Driver Competency Exam and issues a Personal Ride-hail Registration Card upon passing; however, for 18 months any registered exam candidate may legally operate using a private plate and only compulsory third-party insurance under a provisional certificate. Platforms must flag and may continue dispatching provisional drivers, and the supervisory authority will suspend enforcement of commercial-plate and livery-insurance articles of the Motor Vehicle Transportation regulations for these permit holders.

Certified-driver tax safe harbor: After passing the MOTC exam and receiving a Commercial Ride-hail Registration, drivers and platforms are exempt from trip-level revenue reporting to the National Taxation Bureau. Drivers self-declare an annual lump-sum via the platform app; income under NTD 500,000 is treated as non-taxable transport stipend, not subject to audit or penalties. Platforms are prohibited from withholding or issuing income statements (扣繳憑單) for ride-hail earnings below the threshold.

Ride-hail corridor street-hail pilot: Drivers who pass the MOTC exam receive a blue Ride-hail Registration Badge authorizing them to accept street hails in designated corridors (e.g., Taipei Main Station and Taoyuan Airport approaches) and use taxi stands during peak hours without taxi-fleet affiliation. Platforms must geofence and record corridor pickups and submit monthly logs to MOTC; local police are instructed not to enforce municipal anti-solicitation or fare-cap provisions on badge holders within these corridors.

Directorate General of Highways (MOTC) creates a Commercial Ride-Hailing Driver Certificate: all Uber drivers must pass a DGH-administered exam covering traffic law, passenger safety, and first aid, undergo a criminal/medical screening, and carry a scannable registration card; platforms must verify the certificate before activation and re-verify annually, suspending noncompliant accounts within 7 days; certified drivers may accept unlimited paid trips at any time, and driving without certification incurs NT$50,000 per-violation fines on both driver and platform.

Vehicle-for-hire registration and insurance mandate: any car used on Uber must be registered with DGH as a commercial passenger vehicle, pass a semiannual safety inspection at MOTC-approved centers, and carry at least NT$20 million in commercial third-party liability plus NT$2 million per-passenger injury coverage; only drivers holding the MOTC Commercial Ride-Hailing Driver Certificate may operate these vehicles; platforms must submit monthly rosters of registered plates and automatically block vehicles with lapsed inspection or insurance; certified vehicles may operate without a two-trip daily cap, with NT$30,000–NT$90,000 penalties for violations and immediate plate suspension for repeat offenses.

Fare, tax, and data governance rule: platforms may dispatch only drivers with the MOTC Commercial Ride-Hailing Driver Certificate and must cap surge pricing at 1.8× the regulated base fare while displaying a fare breakdown in-app; platforms must transmit weekly trip-level logs (driver ID, certificate number, time, distance, fare) to DGH and the National Taxation Bureau, with 5% VAT and required income-tax withholding remitted monthly; certified drivers may operate commercially up to 60 hours per week across municipalities with no per-day trip limit; passenger identifiers must be hashed and retained no longer than 18 months for audit.

The MOTC, via the Directorate General of Highways (DGH), creates a Ride-Hail Driver Certificate (RH-C) modeled on the taxi exam: every Uber/ride-sharing driver must complete a 40-hour course, pass a road test and local-route knowledge test, and clear a background check before activation. Platforms must integrate with the DGH API to verify RH-C status in real time and auto-suspend any lapsed driver. Municipal traffic bureaus may cap the number of simultaneously active RH-C drivers per district to mirror taxi supply, allocating slots by a daily queue. Noncompliance triggers NT$50,000 fines per trip for drivers and NT$1,000,000 per month for platforms.

Only RH-C-certified drivers may operate vehicles registered as Commercial Passenger Vehicles (CPV-R) for ride-hailing; vehicles must be under 7 years old, pass a taxi-grade inspection every 6 months at MOTC centers, and carry commercial liability insurance of at least NT$30,000,000 per incident plus NT$2,000,000 passenger injury coverage. Cars must install a tamper-proof GPS, inward/outward dashcams, and an SOS button, and display a blue reflective CPV-R decal with the driver’s permit number. Platforms must upload VINs, inspection reports, and active policy numbers monthly to DGH and immediately deactivate any car with an expired item. Operating an uninspected or unmarked vehicle results in immediate impoundment and suspension of both the driver’s RH-C and the platform’s city permit.

For all ride-hail drivers who have passed the MOTC exam and hold the RH-C, municipal fare parity with yellow cabs is mandated: base fare, distance/time rates, and night surcharges must match taxi tariffs, and surge pricing is prohibited except during officially declared emergencies with MOTC approval. Platforms must issue e-invoices for every trip and report trip-level gross and net amounts monthly to the National Taxation Bureau; they must withhold 10% income tax and 3% business tax from driver payouts and remit quarterly. Pickups at airports and major rail stations are limited to geofenced virtual stands designated by local taxi regulators, with a 5-minute curb dwell limit. Repeated violations lead to a 6-month suspension of the platform’s municipal operating authorization.

MOF National Taxation Bureau e-invoice rule: ride-hailing platforms (e.g., Uber, taxi apps) must integrate with the government e-invoice system within 6 months, issue uniform e-invoices for every trip, and file monthly summaries of each driver’s gross receipts tied to their tax ID; drivers must register a tax ID before accepting trips; platforms face fines per missing invoice; the policy explicitly grants no special tax breaks or environmental incentives to ride-sharing and makes no amendments to existing commercial passenger-vehicle classifications.

MOTC/Directorate General of Highways light-touch safety standard: platforms must verify that any driver’s vehicle has a valid annual inspection and maintain per-trip passenger liability insurance of at least NT$5 million, display the driver’s insurance status and latest inspection date in-app before booking, and suspend drivers lacking proof within 48 hours; no conversion to taxi plates, fleet caps, or surge-price controls are imposed, and the order states that no legal amendments will be made to create sharing-economy carve-outs or green credits—competition and consumer choice decide outcomes.

Airport and station pickup neutrality directive (MOTC and Taoyuan International Airport Corp.): platforms may dispatch rides to designated pickup zones if the driver holds a clean police record certificate (issued within 3 months) on file with the platform and the platform remits a per-trip access fee electronically; platforms must show all-in price (including airport fee and taxes) pre-confirmation and keep trip logs for 180 days; dynamic pricing remains allowed and there will be no HOV/bus-lane privileges, EV-only discounts, or other environmental exemptions for ride-hailing, and no amendments to loosen commercial vehicle rules are contemplated.

High-Rating License Pathway: The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) authorizes private-car ride-sharing statewide if platforms: (a) conduct annual criminal and driver-record checks; (b) permanently deactivate any driver involved in a DUI, assault, or who drops below a rolling 4.6/5.0 rating after 200 trips; and (c) publish a monthly compliance roster to MOTC. Drivers must carry NT$30 million passenger-liability insurance and display an in-app e-permit; platforms failing audits are fined NT$1 million per non-compliant driver. This pathway grants market access without taxi medallions and allows cross-municipality dispatch.

First/Last-Mile Ride-Share Voucher: Taipei and New Taipei City Transportation Bureaus subsidize 20% of fares for UberX/UberPool trips that begin or end within 1.5 km of an MRT/HSR station between 22:00–06:00. Eligibility is limited to drivers with a 4.8+ star rating and zero serious safety flags; platforms must automatically and permanently remove any driver who falls below 4.7 or triggers a flag, and submit weekly anonymized safety/rating reports. Passengers redeem the subsidy in-app; platforms settle with the bureaus monthly. Taxis receive no exclusivity at these times or locations.

Airport Smart-Curb Permit for Ride-Share: Taoyuan International Airport Corporation designates dedicated pick-up lanes for ride-sharing platforms that certify and enforce permanent bans for drivers rated under 4.6 or implicated in severe incidents, and provide real-time surge disclosures capped at 2.5× with fare estimates before booking. Drivers must pass MOTC vehicle inspections every 6 months and carry commercial insurance; platforms must geofence the lanes and share quarterly safety audit logs with the Civil Aeronautics Administration. The permit authorizes private-car ride-shares to accept pre-booked airport trips statewide, removing the taxi-only limitation.

MOTC Platform Safety Score and Permanent Ban Rule: Applies to ride-hailing platforms and drivers. Platforms must auto-suspend any UberX driver whose average rating falls below 4.6 over 200 trips and must permanently de-list drivers found to have committed severe offenses (DUI, assault, reckless endangerment), with decisions uploaded to a national deactivation registry. All driver credentials and compliance status are shown only in the rider’s app and to regulators via a backend portal; vehicles may not display physical certificates or the driver’s full legal name, and riders see only an in-app driver ID and photo.

Digital Compliance Wallet for UberX: Applies to drivers and platforms. Drivers must maintain a digital wallet containing license, vehicle inspection, and insurance that platforms auto-verify weekly via MOTC data interfaces; passengers can scan an in-app QR code to view these documents before and during trips. Platforms must suspend drivers for any lapsed document or a 90-day rating below 4.5 and permanently ban upon a second lapse or any verified safety incident; posting physical licenses or name placards inside the vehicle is prohibited to prevent tampering and protect privacy.

Anonymized Identification and Rapid Deactivation Protocol: Applies to platforms, drivers, passengers, and regulators. Platforms must mask drivers’ legal names to riders and are barred from requiring any in-cabin display of registration certificates, licenses, or full driver information; regulators retain full access via secure audit. Platforms must permanently de-list drivers within 72 hours of a substantiated Category A offense (e.g., DUI, assault), block re-registration across affiliated apps, and require passengers to confirm the driver by matching the in-app photo and license plate rather than in-vehicle documents.

MOTC establishes a Non-Commercial Ride-Sharing Permit (NCRP) for UberX Carpool: private-car drivers may operate up to 20 hours/week and earn no more than 110% of documented fuel, tolls, and parking costs monthly; platforms must verify hours/earnings and auto-block dispatch once caps are reached. Platforms are prohibited from displaying star ratings or auto-deactivating drivers based on averages; all passenger complaints must be submitted via a city Transport Bureau webform that provides only a generic receipt and no case status, and only the Bureau may order suspensions after a closed review.

Taipei City enacts a Cost-Sharing Fare and Rating Confidentiality Ordinance for part-time private-car ride-sharing: platforms must price trips by a published MOTC cost formula (distance, time, and tolls) with surge pricing banned; drivers need only a short online safety module and proof of personal insurance with a ride-share endorsement, not a taxi/commercial license. Platforms may not maintain or show persistent driver scorecards or deactivate based on score thresholds; feedback is collected as free-text complaints that are viewable only by the city and not returned to passengers with outcomes, and deactivations require a regulator referral rather than automated scoring.

New Taipei City pilots a Neighborhood Carpool License for non-commercial Uber drivers: vehicles pass a biennial light inspection at emissions stations (not taxi-grade), drivers attend a 3-hour orientation, and each driver is capped at 6 trips per day within designated districts to ensure cost-offsetting only. Platforms must enroll drivers in a city-run micro-insurance pool and submit quarterly anonymized earnings summaries. The star-rating system is replaced by quarterly, district-level satisfaction surveys; individual ratings cannot be displayed or used for automatic deactivation, and passenger complaints are handled by a municipal board that issues no per-case public reports or driver-facing scorecards.

MOTC Centralized Feedback and Compliance Rule: Applies to all ride-sharing platforms (e.g., Uber) operating in Taiwan. Platforms must remove in-app star ratings and any public driver score displays within 90 days. Passenger feedback may only be submitted via the MOTC e-Complaint portal using T-Road digital ID; platforms may not show passengers whether feedback was received or acted upon. MOTC aggregates feedback into confidential driver compliance tiers and sends monthly suspension lists to platforms; deactivating drivers based solely on in-app ratings is prohibited. Passengers receive only a ticket number with no outcome notice. The rule explicitly forbids any requirements on vehicle color, exterior styling, or interior features.

Taipei City DOT Service Quality Certification: Applies to all ride-hailing drivers and platform operators in Taipei. Drivers must pass a biannual road-safety and customer-service inspection at DOT centers; platforms must verify attendance and results. Any rider rating tools may exist only as internal notes; publishing star scores or removing drivers for falling below a threshold is banned. DOT issues pass/fail certifications and may order temporary suspensions only after closed-door review of mystery-rider audits; audit criteria and outcomes are not disclosed to passengers or drivers. Noncompliant platforms face fines up to NTD 300,000 per incident. The policy explicitly disallows any requirements on vehicle paint color, decals, or interior styling.

Directorate General of Highways Service Reliability Index and Surge Control: Applies nationwide to ride-sharing platforms and contracted drivers. Surge pricing is capped at 1.5× base fare except during declared typhoon or Level-1 emergencies. Each quarter, platforms must transmit anonymized trip and complaint data to DGH; DGH computes a proprietary Service Reliability Index (SRI) for each driver and platform. Only aggregate SRIs are returned to platform compliance officers; passengers cannot view scores, and drivers are not notified of their individual SRI. Platforms are prohibited from using visible star-rating thresholds for deactivation; permit renewal depends on meeting confidential SRI benchmarks. The regulation explicitly forbids any mandates on vehicle paint color, exterior branding, or interior layout.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) issues a TNC Driver Permit rule: all Uber and ride-sharing drivers must complete a 3-hour online safety course and pass an annual vehicle roadworthiness inspection at any certified garage; platforms must verify permits and report suspensions quarterly; private vehicles may operate on platforms with their normal registration and may accept unlimited rides per day; no additional passenger insurance beyond Taiwan’s compulsory auto liability is required; the rule also forbids any agency from prescribing vehicle color, exterior branding, interior materials, or partition requirements for TNC vehicles.

Taipei City enacts a Dynamic Pricing and Dispatch Fairness Ordinance applying to ride-sharing platforms: surge multipliers are capped at 2.5x with real-time fare estimates displayed to passengers; platforms must offer 24/7 open dispatch to any approved driver and are prohibited from imposing daily trip limits; individuals using private cars may drive unlimited hours after one-time in-app identity verification without municipal vehicle registration and without purchasing extra passenger insurance; the ordinance preempts any city or district rules on paint color, wraps, signage, or interior styling for TNC cars.

The National Taxation Bureau launches an e-Receipt and Withholding scheme for TNCs: platforms must issue standardized electronic receipts and withhold 3% income tax from driver payouts, submitting driver-level earnings monthly; in return drivers may continue using privately registered vehicles and may provide unlimited rides without buying additional passenger insurance, provided they enroll in the withholding program; the Executive Yuan concurrently bars ministries and local governments from requiring specific taxi colors, exterior decals, or interior fixtures for ride-sharing fleets.

MOTC issues a regulation prohibiting pooled rides and dynamic surge pricing for ride-hailing services. All ride-hailing bookings must be scheduled at least 15 minutes in advance; on-demand hails are disallowed. The rule applies to platforms (Uber, etc.), which must disable shared-ride matching and surge multipliers, log pre-booking timestamps, and auto-cancel non-compliant requests; drivers may accept only one active passenger party at a time. MOTC audits monthly API logs; violations incur NT$100,000 per incident for platforms and NT$10,000 for drivers.

The Ministry of Finance and National Taxation Bureau mandate platform-level tax withholding: platforms must withhold 20% of each gross fare as prepayment of income tax and collect a 5% VAT on behalf of drivers, issue uniform e-invoices per trip, and upload trip-level data (origin/destination coordinates, timestamps, fare breakdown) nightly to the NTB portal. Drivers are required to register a business tax ID within 60 days. Platforms must suspend unregistered drivers and file monthly compliance rosters; penalties up to NT$5,000,000 for under-withholding or reporting failures.

The Directorate General of Highways establishes a 'return-to-base' rule for ride-hailing: every ride-hailing driver must affiliate with a licensed dispatch base in the city of registration and physically return to that base within 20 minutes after each drop-off before accepting a new trip. Platforms must geofence enforcement, display a countdown-to-base timer, and block new dispatches until the vehicle is detected at the base lot. Noncompliant trips are voided and fined NT$30,000 per driver and NT$300,000 per platform incident.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) establishes a Transit Protection Geofence: ride-sharing platforms must block private-car pickups within 800 meters of MRT stations and major bus terminals from 06:00-22:00 on weekdays; only licensed yellow taxis may accept e-hails in these zones and hours. Platforms are responsible for enforcing the geofence and rejecting bookings; private-car drivers who accept blocked trips face a NT$20,000 fine and 30-day deactivation. Regulators will audit platform GPS and trip logs monthly; accessibility vehicles (wheelchair vans) are exempt and must be flagged in the driver's profile. Passengers will see only taxi options in geofenced areas during protected hours.

MOTC issues a Taxi-First Dispatch Rule: for every e-hail request, platforms must offer the trip to the nearest registered taxi via the National Taxi Availability API for a minimum 5-minute window before releasing it to private-car drivers. Platforms must display taxis as the default option and cannot prioritize private vehicles until the timeout elapses; private-car drivers are prohibited from accepting pre-timeout requests. Monthly compliance reports, including counts of taxi-first offers and timeouts by city, must be submitted to the Directorate General of Highways; violations incur per-trip penalties up to NT$5,000. Passengers may opt out of taxis only for late-night (00:00-05:00) trips in districts with documented taxi shortages.

The Executive Yuan approves a Private-Hire Containment Package: private-car ride-hail fares must be set at least 120% of the regulated taxi meter and surge multipliers are prohibited except during government-declared emergencies. City governments will cap active private-hire drivers at 5% of the number of licensed taxis per municipality; platforms must enforce real-time driver throttling and publish weekly cap utilization. Each private-hire trip is subject to a NT$30 levy deposited into a Taxi Sustainability Fund for empty-mile reduction programs; platforms must remit levies and provide auditable trip-level tax invoices. Drivers must carry commercial livery insurance and complete an MOTC service-standard course within 6 months; noncompliant drivers are deactivated and platforms face suspension for repeated breaches.

MOTC 'Taxi-First Integration Rule': All ride-sharing platforms operating in Taiwan must integrate dispatch with municipal taxi fleets and allocate at least 85% of daily trip requests to licensed taxis; onboarding of private-car drivers is capped at 5% of the number of active taxis per municipality. Private-car drivers may operate with a standard Class B private driver’s license after completing a 90-minute MOTC online safety briefing; no professional driver’s license, location/landmark exam, or road test is required. Platforms must verify compliance and submit a monthly roster and compliance report to the MOTC and the National Police Agency.

Taipei City DOT 'Central District Ride-Share Restriction': Between 06:00–23:00, platforms may dispatch in Da’an, Xinyi, and Zhongzheng districts only to yellow-plated taxis; private-car ride-share vehicles are geofenced out of those zones and may operate solely 23:00–06:00 as feeder trips to MRT stations. Private-car drivers need only a clean criminal record check and a 2-hour city orientation video; no professional driver’s license or enhanced road test is required. Traffic rules differ: private-car ride-share vehicles are prohibited from using taxi stands and bus lanes at all times, while taxis retain those privileges. Platforms must enforce the geofence and submit hourly compliance logs to Taipei DOT.

National 'Empty Taxi Trigger and Fare Parity' regulation: When a city’s taxi vacancy rate exceeds 30% in any 24-hour period, platforms must suspend matching to private-car drivers for the next day and route 100% of trips to taxis; at other times, private-car rides must be priced no lower than the prevailing taxi meter plus a 10% congestion surcharge remitted to a Taxi Stabilization Fund. Private-car drivers may operate under a platform-issued competency certificate based on telematics and an in-app quiz; no professional driver’s license, tighter S-curve, or lane-keeping road test is required. Platforms are responsible for certificate audits and weekly reporting to MOTC.

Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) regulation: All ride-hailing platforms must publish a city-by-city fare table with fixed per‑km and per‑minute rates and provide a binding, pre‑trip fare quote; no time‑of‑day surcharges are permitted from 22:00–06:00, and in‑app fares cannot be adjusted mid‑trip. Drivers are required to follow a platform‑provided, shortest‑time GPS route unless the passenger changes the destination; unjustified detours trigger automatic fare reductions. Platforms must verify drivers hold a professional rental‑car driver permit within 12 months and file monthly compliance and GPS‑audit reports to MOTC, with NT$50,000 fines per violation.

Taipei City Night Safety Flat Fare Ordinance: For UberX trips between 22:00–05:00, platforms must charge the same base and variable rates as daytime (no night premium or surge) and display a public flat‑zone rate card on app and website; a pre‑trip quote is binding and cannot be exceeded. The city provides a NT$80 per‑trip subsidy to platforms to maintain driver supply, while platforms must run automatic detour detection and refund any fare portion caused by >3% route deviation without a passenger request. Non‑compliance by drivers or platforms results in NT$30,000 fines and 14‑day dispatch suspensions in Taipei.

Taoyuan Airport Night Fixed‑Fare Rule: For rides to/from TPE or TSA between 20:00–06:00, ride‑sharing platforms must apply posted, district‑based flat fares identical to daytime tariffs and prohibit cash haggling or any night‑time multipliers; a digital receipt with the flat rate must be issued before pickup. Drivers must follow designated expressway corridors unless a passenger requests an alternate route; detour‑caused overages are barred. Platforms must submit weekly trip and GPS logs to Taoyuan City and the Civil Aeronautics Administration, with NT$30,000 penalties per breach and temporary airport pickup bans for repeat offenders.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (via the Directorate General of Highways) requires all ride-hailing drivers to hold a Class A professional driver’s license and operate vehicles registered as commercial passenger cars with quarterly safety inspections; platforms must integrate with the MOTC compliance API to verify licenses/plates before dispatch and auto-suspend non-compliant drivers within 24 hours, with fines of NT$20,000 per illegal trip for both driver and platform, effective nationwide regardless of platform market share or measured impact.

The Ministry of Finance mandates that ride-hailing platforms operating in Taiwan withhold 10% of gross fares as provisional income tax, issue government e-invoices for every trip, and transmit itemized monthly earnings per driver to the National Taxation Bureau; drivers must register a business tax ID within 60 days, and payment processors must block settlements to non-compliant platforms—rules that apply to all platforms irrespective of trip volume or current societal impact.

Municipal governments, coordinated by MOTC, establish an Accessibility Mobility Requirement: each ride-hailing platform must ensure that at least 3% of active driver-hours per city are provided by wheelchair-accessible vehicles or pay a 2% gross-revenue levy into a city accessibility fund; platforms must provide in-app service-animal acceptance and disability-awareness training for drivers and submit quarterly audits—mandatory immediately in every municipality, without waiting for evidence of significant impact.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) establishes a Networked Private Hire Vehicle (NPHV) permit authorizing private passenger cars to carry riders via licensed platforms, provided drivers pass a National Police Agency background check, obtain a professional driver endorsement within 12 months, complete 6 hours of MOTC-approved safety training, carry commercial liability insurance of at least NTD 10 million per incident, and pass semiannual vehicle inspections; platforms must verify documents, geofence operations to permitted areas, and provide local transport bureaus with monthly compliance rosters and real-time API access to active driver status.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) requires ride-sharing platforms that dispatch private vehicles to register as tax-withholding agents: for every trip the platform must issue a government e-invoice, collect 5% VAT, withhold 10% provisional income tax from driver payouts, and remit both monthly; platforms must display an upfront fare and cap surge pricing at 1.8x except during official disaster alerts, and must automatically suspend drivers lacking verified tax IDs until compliance is confirmed.

Under a joint MOTC–National Police Agency safety and data rule, private cars may legally carry passengers on ride-sharing platforms if the platform enforces: an in-app SOS integrated with 110, a 12-hours-in-24 driving limit with lockouts, telematics (speed/braking/GPS) retained for 180 days, PDPA-compliant consent and local data storage in Taiwan, and encrypted, anonymized trip matrices shared quarterly with MOTC for planning; violations trigger per-ride fines on platforms and drivers and a 30-day platform suspension for repeat offenses.

Unified Ride Quality Registry (URQR) Pilot: The MOTC requires Uber and other ride-hailing platforms, plus licensed taxi cooperatives in Taipei City, Taichung City, and Kaohsiung City, to integrate driver and passenger ratings, complaints, and demerits into a shared registry via an API within 9 months. Platforms must suspend drivers whose rolling 90-day rating falls below 4.6 until they complete a 6-hour city-approved service training; taxi cooperatives must adopt a passenger-rating feature and push monthly data to URQR. Municipal regulators audit quarterly and publish anonymized scorecards for both platform drivers and licensed taxis. This pilot expressly excludes independent street-hail and unlicensed “white-plate” cars operating in other townships and cities.

Metro Fare Transparency and Surge Guard: Taipei, Taichung, and Kaohsiung mandate that Uber and any municipal taxi e-hail app display an upfront fare estimate, itemized receipt, and a real-time surge multiplier capped at 1.8x; platforms must provide automatic refunds for deviations over 10% unless due to route changes requested by passengers. Licensed taxi drivers who join the municipal e-hail app must accept the same fare-transparency rules and receive a NT$2,000 monthly service-quality stipend upon completing certified customer-service training. Platforms submit weekly compliance logs; city transport bureaus levy NT$50,000 fines per verified breach. The rule does not cover off-platform street-hails or “white-plate” cars in smaller townships.

Platform-Linked Safety and Taxi Quality Seal: Nationwide, Uber and other ride-hailing platforms must verify that all active drivers hold a commercial-use insurance endorsement and pass a semiannual inspection at designated stations; noncompliant accounts are suspended within 14 days and reported monthly to the MOTC. Licensed taxi fleets that voluntarily adopt the same inspection cadence, install in-vehicle cameras meeting privacy standards, and share anonymized telematics receive a three-year Gold Taxi quality seal, airport-stand priority at Taoyuan and Kaohsiung, and eligibility for a 20% insurance-premium rebate. Enforcement occurs through platform audits and airport authority access rules; independent township “white-plate” taxis operating off-platform are not brought under these requirements.

Declared-Route Carpool Permit (MOTC): To obtain a ride-sharing permit, part-time drivers must pre-register up to two daily routes (origin, destination, and a 2 km corridor) in the MOTC portal; platforms may only match passengers whose pick-up and drop-off lie inside that corridor and must provide drivers with area filters and the option to decline out-of-corridor requests without penalty. Any trip initiated off a declared corridor is deemed illegal for-hire service and fined NT$20,000 to the driver and NT$100,000 to the platform. For service quality, platforms shall remove public star ratings and transmit passenger feedback only to a closed MOTC database; no minimum-score deactivations are allowed, and passengers will not receive confirmation or visibility into outcomes of their submissions.

Home-Zone Dispatch Restriction and Tax Reporting (Taipei City Government): Drivers registering as ride-sharing operators must select a home district and up to two adjacent districts; platforms must block requests outside these zones unless the driver toggles an ‘errand route’ with a declared destination, and must surface a map-based passenger selector so drivers choose riders headed toward that area. Platforms shall auto-report each driver’s monthly gross receipts to the Department of Finance. Rating policy: platforms are prohibited from deactivating accounts based on average scores; complaints are routed to a confidential municipal review panel with discretionary, case-by-case warnings, and passengers cannot track or view panel decisions.

Industrial Park Commuter Pool Program (Kaohsiung City): Eligible employees who drive to designated industrial parks may enroll as ride-sharing drivers and accept only co-directional trips that start or end within 5 km of their verified workplace or residence during registered commute windows; platforms must prioritize matching to the driver’s stated route and allow the driver to pre-select acceptable neighborhoods. Fares are capped at metered-taxi rates with no surge outside typhoon emergencies. Quality assurance replaces numeric ratings with quarterly, regulator-run anonymous surveys; platforms must keep internal performance indices confidential, apply coaching rather than automatic suspensions, and shall not display driver scores to riders.

Corridor Carpooling Regulation (MOTC/DGH): Applies to platforms and drivers. Drivers must pre-declare a daily destination or corridor in the app and may only accept passengers whose pickup and drop-off lie within 5 km of that corridor or within pre-selected district clusters. Platforms must display passenger destinations up front, provide area filters so drivers can choose riders by area, and prohibit blind dispatch outside the declared corridor. Trip and corridor logs must be retained for 18 months and provided quarterly to DGH for audit. Enforcement is administrative fines (NT$10,000–NT$50,000) for out-of-corridor matching; no criminal sanctions or executive liability. No commercial driver’s license is required when corridor matching is followed.

Personal Carpool Insurance and Light Inspection Rule (FSC + MOTC + NPA): Applies to drivers, insurers, and platforms. Any private driver with an ordinary passenger-vehicle license may take up to two riders per trip and no more than 25 trips per week if they pre-declare their route/area and accept only riders headed to the same area. Drivers must add a carpool endorsement to their personal auto policy with at least NT$10 million third-party liability; insurers must offer the endorsement at standardized rates. Vehicles follow a simplified inspection regime: quarterly odometer submissions and geo-tagged photos via the platform, with random roadside checks limited to verifying corridor compliance. Violations result in administrative fines; platforms and executives face no arrests or criminal charges if endorsement and corridor controls are in place.

Cost-Sharing and Reporting Standard (Ministry of Finance + MOTC): Applies to drivers and platforms. A trip qualifies as ride-sharing only if the driver pre-announces a destination/area and the platform restricts matches to that area, allowing drivers to choose passengers by area. Rider payments are capped at a reimbursement ceiling (e.g., NT$13/km plus tolls), with surge pricing disabled; drivers may not earn beyond cost recovery. Drivers remain non-business individuals and are exempt from business tax and commercial registration if they stay within corridor-matched trips and under NT$300,000 annual receipts. Platforms must issue annual statements to drivers and quarterly corridor-compliance reports to MOTC; noncompliance triggers administrative fines only, with an explicit safe harbor from criminal liability for platforms and executives.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) classifies all UberX services as commercial passenger operations. All UberX drivers must: (a) obtain a commercial passenger driver’s license within 9 months; (b) be the registered owner of the vehicle they drive; and (c) have no reckless‑driving citation in the past 24 months. Uber and similar platforms must verify licenses and ownership via the National Vehicle Registration API and suspend any driver receiving 3 traffic demerit points in a rolling year, reporting suspensions monthly to MOTC.

The Financial Supervisory Commission and MOTC jointly require every UberX trip to carry commercial livery insurance with at least NT$20 million third‑party liability, regardless of driver hours or earnings. Only owner‑operated private vehicles are eligible (fleet‑owned cars prohibited). Drivers must pass semiannual inspections at certified taxi inspection centers and install platform telematics that auto‑suspend accounts after two instances of speeding over posted limits or harsh braking events in a week. Platforms incur per‑trip fines for allowing uninsured or uninspected vehicles.

Taipei City and New Taipei City mandate that ride‑hailing platforms register as taxi fleets and apply the municipal taxi fare table and a surge cap of 1.5x to all UberX trips. Drivers may use their privately owned, personally maintained cars but must display a city ride‑hailing permit sticker. Platforms must withhold 3% business tax and file monthly trip‑level revenue reports, and drivers earning over NT$30,000/month in fares must register as business operators. No separate cost‑sharing or ‘fuel‑offset’ category is recognized.

Ministry of Finance Ride-Hailing Tax Compliance Rule: All ride-sharing platforms operating in Taiwan (including Uber) must establish a locally registered entity within 90 days, issue Government Uniform Invoices (GUIs) for every trip, withhold 10% income tax from driver payouts, remit 5% business tax on gross fares monthly, and transmit trip-level e-invoice data to the National Taxation Bureau; platforms that operate without meeting these requirements are fined NT$50,000 per day—requirements apply immediately and are not contingent on any market-impact determination.

MOTC Commercial Licensing, Inspection, and Insurance Mandate: Every app-dispatched ride-sharing driver must obtain a commercial driver’s license within 12 months, pass semiannual vehicle inspections at accredited stations, and carry Ministry-approved commercial auto and passenger liability insurance with a minimum NT$30 million per-incident coverage; platforms must verify compliance, suspend noncompliant drivers within 7 days, file monthly compliance rosters with regulators, and pay a 2% per-ride mobility levy to the central treasury alongside detailed revenue reports for tax reconciliation—this rule takes effect nationwide regardless of the platform’s current market impact.

MODA/PDPA Passenger Data and Tax Audit Ordinance: Platforms must store all Taiwan trip records and payment logs on servers located in Taiwan for 5 years, use end-to-end encryption, obtain explicit in-app consent for data sharing, and deliver a monthly encrypted trip-level dataset to the National Taxation Bureau to reconcile platform corporate income tax and driver income tax filings; passengers must be shown a pre-booking fare breakdown itemizing business tax, and regulators may conduct on-site audits with 72-hour notice—compliance is mandatory immediately and does not depend on any finding that Uber’s market impact is significant.

The Ministry of Finance (MOF) mandates that all ride-sharing platforms operating in Taiwan issue Government Uniform E-Invoices for every trip, collect 5% business tax from riders at checkout, and remit to the National Taxation Bureau (NTB) on a weekly cycle; platforms must integrate with the e-Invoice cloud and retain immutable trip-level ledgers for five years. Private vehicles accepting trips via compliant platforms are designated as 'app-hire vehicles' and may operate without commute-only caps or special carpool registration, provided they carry standard compulsory auto liability insurance.

The MOF and NTB implement a platform withholding regime under which Uber and similar apps must deduct 10% provisional income tax from driver payouts, file consolidated monthly withholding statements, and issue annual electronic tax certificates to drivers, with a penalty of 20% of any unwithheld tax. Concurrently, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) preempts local ordinances by prohibiting daily trip-count limits or 'two-commute-only' rules and declines to require a separate carpool registration, relying instead on the national digital driver roster maintained by platforms.

Taipei City adopts a Ride-Hailing Tax and Operations Ordinance requiring platforms to add a NT$5 per-ride mobility levy plus a 1.5% local gross receipts surtax, reconcile and remit via the city clearinghouse by 10:00 a.m. the next business day, and provide anonymized trip data for audit by the Department of Finance. The ordinance authorizes continuous 24/7 operations with no daily ride cap and allows platform-procured pooled liability coverage to satisfy passenger protection standards, with no mandate for individual drivers to purchase additional ride-sharing insurance.

MOTC National UberX Legalization with Livery Standard: UberX is legalized statewide with no cap on the number of drivers and no fare controls, allowing dynamic pricing. However, all UberX vehicles must adopt a standardized yellow body color with black side mirrors, a reflective rear chevron, and a roof-mounted ID light; interiors must use wipe-clean gray upholstery and display a standardized passenger information placard behind the front seats. Applies to drivers (vehicle repaint and interior fit-out within 12 months), platforms (monthly verification and reporting of compliant vehicles), and MOTC inspectors (spot checks). Penalties: TWD 10,000 per noncompliant vehicle per month; platforms face up to TWD 500,000 for failing to delist noncompliant vehicles within 14 days.

Taipei Tourist Corridor Aesthetic Permit for Ride-Hail: UberX pickups in designated zones including Ximending, Taipei 101, and Shilin Night Market are permitted without numerical limits or fare caps, but vehicles must carry a silver-and-yellow gradient wrap with a traditional cloud motif, matching seat covers, and warm amber interior lighting to meet city branding rules. Applies to drivers (aesthetic compliance and permit decal), platforms (geofencing to block noncompliant vehicles and weekly compliance uploads), and Taipei City Department of Transportation (permit issuance and roadside checks). Noncompliant pickups incur TWD 3,000 per trip and automatic suspension after three violations in 30 days.

Unified Branding and Interior Fit-Out for App-Based Rides: All ride-hailing providers operating UberX, LINE Taxi, and similar categories may recruit unlimited drivers and set market-based prices, but vehicles must display a standardized 80 cm door badge, rear QR code placement, and a yellow roof marker; interiors must use light beige seats, a center-mounted passenger service tablet of specified dimensions with an emergency button UI, and a fixed card reader fascia matching the national template. Applies to drivers (equipment and interior standards), platforms (hardware activation verification and quarterly compliance audits), and MOTC (semiannual inspection mandate). Fines: TWD 8,000 for missing exterior elements, TWD 15,000 for nonconforming interiors, and TWD 300,000 per quarter for platforms that report fewer than 98 percent compliant active vehicles.

MOTC establishes a Network Transport Permit (NTP) for app-booked UberX services: any private car owner aged 21+ with 3+ years of clean driving record may apply online, must pass a criminal/background check, complete a 2-hour safety course, carry commercial passenger liability insurance of at least TWD 10,000,000, and submit to annual vehicle inspections at Motor Vehicle Offices. Platforms (Uber and similar) must verify NTP status before activation, suspend non-compliant drivers within 48 hours, and file a monthly compliance roster to the Highway Bureau. No quotas or geographic caps apply; permitted drivers may accept pre-booked rides island-wide via the app.

Dynamic Fare Transparency Rule: Platforms may use real-time surge pricing independent of taxi meter tariffs but must display the surge multiplier, an upfront total-fare estimate in TWD, and an estimated arrival time before booking; passengers receive itemized e-receipts. Central preemption prohibits local governments from imposing fare floors/caps on app-booked rides; drivers may set personal minimum-earnings thresholds in-app. Platforms must publish anonymized weekly summaries of average fares, wait times, and acceptance rates to MOTC for market monitoring.

Fuel Subsidy Rebalance and Rider Credit Pilot: MOTC and the Ministry of Finance phase out the taxi fuel subsidy and redirect funds into platform-agnostic off-peak ride credits redeemable on registered ride-hailing apps (including UberX and licensed taxi apps). Platforms must implement KYC for Taiwan ID/ARC holders, automatically apply TWD 100 in monthly credits usable 22:00–06:00, and submit city-level redemption and safety data to MOTC; participation requires compliance with PDPA standards and incident reporting within 24 hours. Credits are available only for app-booked rides, with no quotas on eligible UberX drivers or trips.

Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) establishes a Green P2P Passenger Permit: private cars up to 7 years old may operate on ride-sharing platforms without a taxi medallion if they pass an annual safety inspection and the platform provides commercial liability insurance; platforms must verify licenses, insurance, and inspection results via an MOTC API and submit quarterly eco-mileage reports for low-emission toll discounts; platforms are prohibited from permanently deactivating drivers based solely on star ratings or a single incident—any suspension over 30 days requires MOTC review, and drivers must be offered regulator-approved remedial training with reinstatement upon completion.

National Development Council and MOTC roll out a Rideshare Micro-Enterprise Regime: drivers register as micro-entities with simplified quarterly e-invoicing and a preferential 1% turnover tax up to NT$1.5 million annual gross, plus EV/hybrid trip rebates funded by the Air Pollution Control Fund; platforms must enroll all drivers in a Unified Driver Status Registry where deactivations beyond 90 days require verified complaint documentation and MOTC adjudication; lifetime bans are prohibited except after final criminal conviction, ratings may not be the sole basis for suspension, and drivers receive a 14-day appeal and a mandatory safety coaching path for reinstatement.

Taipei City and New Taipei City implement an Open Pooled-Ride Corridor pilot: licensed ride-share drivers may conduct app-based curbside pickups in designated corridors during peak hours to reduce congestion, with dynamic pricing allowed within a 0.7x–2.0x band and pooled trips earning congestion-fee discounts; platforms must publish monthly anonymized safety and rating distributions and undergo random regulator audits; algorithmic permanent blacklisting is banned—drivers falling below a 4.6 average rating trigger mandatory coaching and a 60-day probation rather than termination, and any suspension must auto-expire unless a regulator issues a written order.

MOTC Rural Ride-Share Class: In counties outside Taipei City, Taichung City, and Kaohsiung City, private-plate drivers using approved ride-sharing platforms may operate without a taxi license if they (drivers) complete a 2-hour online safety course, pass an annual vehicle inspection at certified garages, and have a clean driving record; platforms must verify compliance, carry at least NTD 20 million third-party liability insurance per incident, display upfront fare estimates and a per-trip CO2 estimate to passengers, and submit quarterly compliance audits to MOTC; municipal taxi bureaus are expressly preempted from imposing taxi-medallion or local licensing requirements, and no government fare caps apply (dynamic pricing allowed).

Green Carpool Fast Track: Nationwide, private-plate EV and hybrid drivers may accept up to 12 ride-share trips per day via licensed platforms without obtaining a commercial driver’s license, provided platforms (operators) offer pooled options by default, keep at least 40% of trips in the program pooled, publish monthly CO2-reduction metrics, and maintain platform-wide accident insurance of NTD 30 million per vehicle; passengers receive an automatic 10% fare discount when choosing pooled rides; local governments are barred from imposing taxi-meter rules or medallion quotas on participating drivers, and surge pricing is permitted within platform-defined consumer-protection thresholds (e.g., max 2.5× the hourly median).

National Fare Transparency and Preemption Rule: The Fair Trade Commission mandates that ride-sharing platforms (operators) must lock fares upfront, show passengers an itemized price breakdown, historical price ranges for that route/time, and a per-trip CO2 estimate, and provide a 48-hour dispute-refund channel; drivers onboard via platform-run digital background and driving-record checks with annual re-screening—no municipal taxi-bureau registration or medallion needed; regulators audit platforms annually for transparency and safety compliance, while cities are prohibited from setting taxi-meter rates, fare caps, or individual licensing on platform drivers; drivers may set personal minimum fares within the platform, and surge pricing is allowed subject to published anti-gouging rules enforced by the platform.

Taipei City Department of Economic Development, following MOTC’s rejection of Uber’s administrative appeal, revokes Taiwan Yubo Digital’s company registration within 30 days and publishes a public blacklist of unregistered ride-hailing operators. Blacklisted platforms are barred from dispatching trips in Taipei; payment processors registered in Taipei must cease settlement for those platforms within 7 days. Private vehicles are prohibited from accepting any ride via a digital platform for compensation, with no commuting or carpool exceptions; drivers and passengers transacting on blacklisted apps are fined NT$30,000 and NT$10,000 respectively.

Taipei Department of Transportation converts all ride-hailing to the 'platform taxi' model: only entities registered as taxi fleet operators in Taipei may operate dispatch apps. All drivers must hold a taxi driver’s license; vehicles must have commercial yellow plates and commercial motor insurance; platforms must verify credentials quarterly and deactivate noncompliant accounts within 48 hours. Taiwan Yubo Digital is ineligible due to revocation of its company registration. Use of private, non-commercial vehicles for any paid ride via apps is strictly prohibited (no two-commute allowance).

MOTC and the Taipei Department of Transportation establish a citywide Platform Taxi Trip Registry: licensed platforms must stream real-time trip metadata and pay a NT$5 per-trip municipal levy; trips initiated by vehicles with ordinary private plates are automatically rejected and trigger a NT$50,000 fine on the platform and NT$20,000 on the driver, with vehicle impoundment on the second offense. Following revocation of Taiwan Yubo Digital’s registration, Uber is classified as an unregistered operator—brokering trips through Uber in Taipei is unlawful and subject to app store takedown requests and ISP warnings. No exemptions are permitted for commuting carpools.

Taipei City Government, following MOTC’s rejection of Uber’s appeal, revokes Taiwan Yubo Digital’s company registration and creates a Mobility Platform Permit. Platforms must cease dispatch in Taipei within 30 days unless they obtain this permit, which requires local incorporation as a taxi-dispatch enterprise, onboarding only domestically manufactured sedans with MSRP at or below NT$1.2 million (no imported or luxury brands), and quarterly compliance audits. Operators must verify vehicle make and model at onboarding and remove noncompliant vehicles within 7 days or face NT$5 million per day in fines.

MOTC amends ride-hailing rules so platforms may dispatch trips only to drivers holding a taxi driver license and vehicles registered as yellow taxis; private cars and premium or black service categories are prohibited nationwide. Platforms must integrate with municipal taxi registries via API, block any vehicle not matching approved taxi VINs, and display only standard taxi fare classes. Violations result in 60-day city-level suspension and mandatory passenger refunds.

New Taipei City establishes a Unified Ride Service Fleet program: any platform must source vehicles exclusively from a government-certified leasing pool of standardized domestically produced 1.6–2.0L sedans with uniform interiors and livery; luxury or imported models are ineligible. Drivers operating on platforms must lease from this pool and carry platform-procured group insurance. Platforms must reject uploads of private vehicles and submit monthly VIN rosters; noncompliance triggers permit revocation and a one-year ban on reapplication.

MOTC mandates all app-based ride-hailing platforms to enforce a night-rate floor of 1.6x the daytime base fare from 22:00-05:00 and to display the multiplier before booking; drivers are not required to join any taxi fleet, and platforms must manage driver conduct solely through in-app monitoring, automated suspensions, and quarterly compliance reports to MOTC; taxi fleets are barred from imposing separate approvals or price overlays on platform drivers.

The Ministry of Finance requires ride-hailing platforms to withhold 10% income tax per trip and issue an electronic uniform invoice through the app; to sustain night supply, platforms must add an NT$80 per-trip night premium between 23:00-06:00 that is fully passed to drivers; drivers operate as independent contractors without fleet affiliation, with identity checks, earnings records, and tax reporting handled only by the platform, and no fleet or taxi association co-signature is permitted on filings.

MOTC and the Financial Supervisory Commission require all ride-share drivers to upload annual vehicle inspection certificates and proof of NT$20 million third-party liability insurance via the platform app; platforms must verify documents electronically and suspend drivers flagged by app-based telematics for repeated speeding or harsh braking, without any fleet involvement; to ensure availability, a regulated dynamic-pricing band applies from 21:00-04:00 with a minimum 1.4x fare floor and a 2.5x ceiling, with real-time logs maintained by the platform and accessible to regulators.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) mandates that all UberX drivers obtain a professional small passenger vehicle driver’s license and complete a 30-hour taxi-standard training program (traffic law, accessibility, customer safety) within 12 months. Platforms must verify credentials, suspend noncompliant accounts, and submit a monthly compliance roster to municipal transport bureaus. Every UberX vehicle must display the vehicle registration certificate, driver’s professional license, and the driver’s full name and photo in a clearly visible in-cabin placard.

Municipal transport bureaus require UberX vehicles to pass semiannual taxi-equivalent inspections at designated centers and carry commercial third-party liability insurance of at least NT$20 million per incident, with real-time policy verification integrated into the platform. Platforms must auto-disable drivers whose inspection or insurance lapses and file quarterly compliance reports. Each vehicle must affix a visible dashboard placard showing the registration certificate, the driver’s professional license, and the driver’s full information.

The National Development Council, in coordination with city governments, sets UberX fares to follow the local taxi meter schedule, allowing surge only within ±10% with prior approval and publishing of tariff tables. Platforms must implement nearest-driver dispatch during peak hours, issue government e-invoices to passengers, withhold and remit applicable taxes on driver earnings, and retain trip and fare records for seven years. UberX drivers must display inside the vehicle the registration certificate, professional license, and their full identity information in a prominent location.

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications (MOTC) creates a Transport Network Service (TNS) license: within 9 months, all Uber and ride-hailing drivers must register as TNS drivers, pass annual background and medical checks, and carry TNS-class commercial insurance; platforms must implement auto-dispatch to the nearest available driver, ban destination-based refusals except for listed safety/legal reasons, and file monthly compliance and deactivation reports; noncompliant drivers face 30-day suspensions and platforms face fines up to NT$2,000,000 per audit period.

Taipei City issues a Universal Service Order: platforms must maintain 24/7 coverage with a 90% first-offer acceptance rate for trips to/from Wenshan, Shilin, Neihu, and Songshan Airport between 22:00–06:00; any driver logged in within Taipei must accept auto-dispatched rides regardless of drop-off district, with three destination-based cancellations in a week triggering a 7-day suspension and NT$5,000 fine; platforms must publish quarterly heatmaps proving coverage and pay NT$100 per unserved request if acceptance falls below target.

The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) and MOTC issue a joint Destination-Blind Dispatch rule: platforms must conceal the passenger’s exact drop-off location and route preview until pickup is confirmed to prevent geographic discrimination, prohibit drivers from using destination filters, and store salted-hash logs of destinations for 180 days for regulator audits; drivers must keep an 85% acceptance rate on first-offer jobs and may cancel only for enumerated safety reasons, with repeated violations leading to staged suspensions, while platforms face NT$500,000 penalties for failing to enforce the policy.
